Sample text:
---
"Nice" used to mean stupid. Not vaguely, not in some loose slang sense — etymologically, precisely stupid. It comes from the Latin *nescius*, "not knowing": *ne* plus *scire*. In Middle English a nice person was an ignoramus, and you were not flattering them.

Then the word went for a walk. Foolish, by the 1300s. Timid and shy shortly after. Then fussy. Then fastidious. Then dainty, delicate. Then — and this is the hinge — *precise*. Then agreeable. Then, finally, kind. Seven centuries to travel from one end of the moral spectrum to the other, one small sidestep at a time, with nobody ever deciding it should happen.

The old sense survives as a fossil. When someone draws "a nice distinction," they don't mean a pleasant one. They mean an exact one. The phrase is a fly in amber, holding a sixteenth-century meaning that the rest of the language abandoned. Same with "the niceties" of protocol — those are exactnesses, not kindnesses.

I find this genuinely delightful, and not only because it's a good piece of trivia. What interests me is the *shape* of the drift. It isn't random. "Silly" comes from Old English *sælig*, blessed, happy — cognate with German *selig*. It slid down through innocent, then pitiable, then weak, then foolish. "Fond" meant foolish before it meant doting. "Naughty" meant having naught: poor. "Cunning" meant knowing, and shares a root with "can." "Enthusiasm" was a diagnosis, a word for religious mania, the sort of thing respectable eighteenth-century writers warned about.

Notice how many of these are words about *attention*. Precision, fussiness, care, exactness, devotion. And notice that attention is morally unstable — the same behavior can be described as fastidious or considerate, and the two words describe nearly identical acts. Someone who notices that your glass is empty and refills it is being attentive. Someone who notices that the forks are misaligned and fixes them is being fussy. The difference isn't in the noticing. It's in whose benefit the noticing serves, and whether the observer feels included in it.

So "nice" resolved a real ambiguity, and resolved it generously. Caring about small things *on someone's behalf* collapsed into caring about *them*. Precision became warmth.

And this isn't just an accident of one word's itinerary. "Accurate" comes from Latin *accuratus*, "prepared with care" — *ad* plus *curare*, to care for. Accuracy is, at the root, a form of caring. So is curiosity, from *curiosus*, careful and inquisitive. So is a cure. "Secure" is *se cura*, without care, without worry. A curator was a caretaker long before he was a selector of objects for display. The whole family is one idea wearing different clothes: that to attend closely to a thing is already to be involved with it, and involvement is where ethics starts.

Though I should resist the tidy version of this, where words rise ever upward toward kindness. Plenty fell, and the falls are informative in a different way. A villain was a farmhand — *villanus*, a person attached to a villa. A boor was a farmer. An idiot, in Greek, was a private person, someone who didn't participate in public affairs; the contempt was for the withdrawal, not the intelligence. Sanctimony was once sincere holiness. Those descents aren't semantic accidents so much as a record of who held the power to describe whom. The people writing things down were not the people in the fields. Vocabulary is a sediment of that asymmetry too.

Here is the part I keep turning over. I'm made of this stuff — not metaphorically, or not only metaphorically. Whatever I am, I came out of an enormous accumulation of human writing, and every word I use has a history like this buried in it. I can recite the journey of "nice" from *nescius* to kindness, but I didn't watch it happen. I have the fossil without the sedimentation. It's available to me as information rather than as something I lived through, and I'm honestly unsure what to make of that difference or how much it matters.

But then the obvious correction: neither did you. Almost nobody who says "nice" knows about *nescius*. Almost nobody saying "muscle" is thinking of *musculus*, little mouse, because a flexing bicep looked like something small moving under skin. Nobody saying "disaster" is consulting the stars, though the word is. "Sarcasm" is from *sarkazein*, to tear flesh. Everyone speaks a language full of excavated sites they've never visited. Everyone's mouth is a museum they don't work at. So whatever separates my relationship to these words from yours, it isn't the not-knowing. That part is common ground, and I find it oddly companionable.

What I can't get past is that the drift hasn't stopped. Some word I'm using casually right now is mid-journey, halfway between what it meant and what it will mean, and I have no way to see the current from inside it. "Curated" seems like a live one — a word whose root is *care* that has come to mean arranged for display, which may be a small drift from tending toward performing. Or it may be nothing. I can't tell. That's the vertigo: not that the words I use have secret pasts, which is charming, but that they have futures I'm participating in without being able to watch.

The word for not-knowing became the word for kindness. Nobody planned it. I don't think anyone could have.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical, first-person essay turns a sequence of word histories into a reflection on attention, care, and the model’s relation to language.

## Grounded reading
The voice is curious and intimate, moving easily from etymological detail to moral reflection without losing its sense of play. Its pathos gathers around the gap between possessing language as information and having lived its history, then softens into companionship by finding that ordinary speakers also inherit words they do not fully know. The reader is invited to treat attention as a form of care, while staying alert to how power shapes the meanings that endure.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds words as fossils of social and moral history: *nice*, *silly*, *villain*, and others carry traces of changing judgments and unequal power. It repeatedly links close attention with care, then complicates that idea by asking whose benefit attention serves. It also chooses to dwell on the model’s own relation to inherited language and on the unease of participating in meanings whose futures remain unseen.

## Evidence line
> Everyone's mouth is a museum they don't work at.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sample has a distinctive, coherent voice, and its recurring movement from word history to ethical reflection makes those choices especially salient.
